articles.summary: US orders departure of personnel from Saudi Arabia, citing Houthi threat  Al JazeeraU.S. pulls diplomats from Saudi Arabia as it reportedly readies Iran strikes after midterms  CNBCUS pulls personnel from Saudi Arabia as kingdom comes under Houthi fire  Fox NewsU.S. troops and diplomats evacuating Middle East posts, sources say  NBC NewsWashington orders US embassy staff, families to leave Saudi Arabia  Yahoo
articles.full_text:
The United States Department of State has ordered the departure of nonemergency government employees and their family members from its mission in Saudi Arabia as attacks by the Iran-aligned Houthi movement on the kingdom have ramped up.
“Iranian-supported Houthis have increasingly engaged in hostilities against Saudi Arabia, including attacks on civilian airports and other critical infrastructure resulting in civilian casualties and severe travel disruptions,” State Department spokesperson Tommy Pigott said in a social media post on Wednesday.
“The safety and security of Department personnel and their families remain our highest priority, and we will continue to take all necessary steps to protect and support them,” he added.
Pigott said that an earlier media report on US plans for the departure of some personnel and family members at US embassies across the Gulf was “inaccurate”.
More departures possible
Four US officials told the Reuters news agency that US missions in other Gulf states would also be ordering family members to leave.
The US had returned some diplomatic personnel to the region in recent months after many were pulled out when Tehran launched attacks on US facilities after the US-Israeli war on Iran began in late February.
The latest withdrawals follow an escalation of fighting in Yemen, opening another front in the regional conflict triggered by the war. The conflict has snarled global energy trade and hurt Gulf economies.
The US embassy in Riyadh issued a security alert on Wednesday about possible further attacks by the Houthis on Saudi Arabia after recent deadly strikes, including on Riyadh’s airport.
The embassy and a CIA station hosted there came under attack by drones in early March, as Iran began launching attacks across the region.

articles.title: At least 2 killed in Houthi attack on Saudi Arabia’s Dammam airport
articles.summary: At least two people were killed and eight others wounded in a late-night attack on Saudi Arabia’s Dammam airport, the civil aviation authority said Thursday, as Houthi strikes from...
articles.full_text:
At least two people were killed and eight others wounded in a late-night attack on Saudi Arabia’s Dammam airport, the civil aviation authority said Thursday, as Houthi strikes from Yemen intensify.
A Saudi and an Indian man were killed in the attack Wednesday, the General Authority of Civil Aviation (GACA) said in a statement, updating an earlier death toll. Damage to the airport was being assessed, it added.
The authority said the eight injured include one Saudi citizen, two Indian nationals, two Yemenis, two Bangladeshis, and one Nepalese national.
The injuries range from minor to severe, and they are receiving the necessary medical care at several hospitals, it added.
GACA noted that airport operations had resumed and air traffic had returned to normal.
It added that, in coordination with the relevant security authorities, work was continuing to assess the damage and take all necessary measures to ensure the safety of passengers and workers and maintain the security and safety of the kingdom's civil aviation system.
The authority did not specify the nature of the attack.
The attack comes amid escalating hostilities between Yemen's Houthi group and the Saudi-led coalition, including attacks targeting Saudi airports and energy facilities. They forced Riyadh to shut its main airport and postpone a major investment conference.
A total of 22 people have been killed in attacks on Saudi airports this month, according to an AFP tally of official figures.
King Fahd International Airport previously came under attack on Oct. 11, prompting damage assessments and safety inspections.
Earlier Wednesday, Saudi Arabia's Energy Ministry said two people were killed and two others injured by falling debris after air defenses intercepted a drone targeting an Aramco facility at the Shaybah oil field in the Eastern Province.
The debris caused a fire in a contractor's vehicle, but operations at the oil field were unaffected, according to the ministry.
The Saudi-led coalition also announced Wednesday that it intercepted and destroyed five drones launched toward the kingdom, including in the Eastern Province and Medina region.
A Houthi maritime blockade in the Red Sea is also threatening oil shipments from Saudi Arabia, the world's biggest exporter of crude.
The Houthi attacks follow the collapse in July of a yearslong truce in Yemen's civil war, where the Iran-backed group is fighting the government supported by a Saudi-led coalition.
The Houthis declared a maritime blockade of Saudi Arabia and began hitting its ships, territory and oil facilities, before launching a major offensive in September in which they seized government-held territory along the Red Sea coast.
In response, the Saudi air force has frequently targeted areas under Houthi control, which includes much of impoverished Yemen.

articles.title: US orders some diplomats to leave Saudi Arabia as Houthi attacks escalate - BBC
articles.summary: US orders some diplomats to leave Saudi Arabia as Houthi attacks escalate  BBC
articles.full_text:
The US State Department has ordered some diplomats and their families to leave Saudi Arabia as attacks escalate, with three people killed in strikes across the country.
Saudi authorities said debris from a drone intercepted during an attempted attack on an oil field killed two people, while one person died after a strike at the King Fahd International Airport in Dammam.
Conflict between Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis and Saudi Arabia has been rising in the past month.
The Houthis have responded to Saudi strikes by launching missiles and drones at airports, energy facilities and military bases in Saudi Arabia. A recent strike on Riyadh's international airport was the deadliest in the kingdom in years.
"The US Department of State issued an ordered departure for non-emergency US government employees and their family members in Saudi Arabia," a state department spokesperson said in a statement.
"Iranian-supported Houthis have increasingly engaged in hostilities against Saudi Arabia, including attacks on civilian airports and other critical infrastructure resulting in civilian casualties and severe travel disruptions," it added.
The spokesperson also warned "the hostilities have the potential to escalate rapidly".
In the latest attack on the King Fahd International Airport eight people sustained injuries that ranged from "minor to serious", officials said.
No details of the attack have yet been given, but the strike comes after airports in Saudi Arabia have been repeatedly targeted by Houthi forces.
The energy ministry has also not said who had launched the drone aimed at the Shaybah oil field near the border with the United Arab Emirates that left two people injured.
Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began when the Houthis ousted the government from the capital, Sanaa, in 2014. Conflicts escalated in 2015, after a Saudi-led military coalition tried to restore the government's rule.
An informal ceasefire had been in place for the past four years, but it unravelled in July after the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea.
The Houthis said they were retaliating for what they have called a Saudi blockade of their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom.
The group's "maritime embargo" in the Bab al-Mandab Strait along Yemen's south-western coast has contributed to a surge in global oil prices because Saudi Arabia had been relying on the Red Sea for oil exports since the US and Israel's war with Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz in the Gulf.

articles.title: Iran warns US, allies of retaliation over attacks on officials
articles.summary: Iran warned Wednesday that U.S. political assets and infrastructure belonging to countries involved in any renewed war against Tehran could become targets of retaliation if Iranian...
articles.full_text:
Iran warned Wednesday that U.S. political assets and infrastructure belonging to countries involved in any renewed war against Tehran could become targets of retaliation if Iranian officials are assassinated or civilians killed, according to a senior security official cited by the semi-official Fars News Agency.
The Tehran-based official said Iran assumes that the U.S. and Israel will launch another attack and considers Washington’s diplomatic gestures "unreliable.”
The official said this perception had intensified following remarks by U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio in Athens, which Tehran interpreted as giving a historical and civilizational justification for Washington’s war against Iran.
According to the official, Iranian political and intellectual leaders have increasingly concluded that US Middle East policy is directed by Israel, which they believe is preventing Washington from pursuing a diplomatic solution.
The official claimed that Israel takes priority in U.S. President Donald Trump’s regional policies.
Iran already considers itself at war with the U.S. and views Washington’s economic and naval blockade, along with restrictions on Iranian airspace, as a continuation of the military aggression that began on Feb. 28, the official said.
He added that growing pressure from different segments of Iranian society was pushing authorities toward "decisive action” to break the blockade under what Tehran considers its right to self-defense.
According to the official, Iran has instructed various operational units that, in the event of another large-scale conflict involving the assassination of Iranian officials and the killing of civilians, it would consider U.S. political assets and the infrastructure of countries participating in the war as "legitimate targets.”
The warning comes amid heightened tensions between Tehran and Washington over the U.S. naval blockade and restrictions on maritime traffic through the Strait of Hormuz.
The US and Israel launched military strikes against Iran on Feb. 28, triggering a wider regional conflict. Despite subsequent diplomatic efforts, disagreements over the blockade and security arrangements in the strategic waterway have continued.
The warning also follows an Israeli media report on Wednesday that dozens of Israeli fighter jets flew close to Iran’s border earlier this week, with U.S. sources suggesting the operation may have been intended to provoke an Iranian response.

articles.title: Return to US-Iran war looms after 7 tankers damaged in Hormuz
articles.summary: Seven oil tankers caught fire or were damaged in the Strait of Hormuz overnight into Thursday after being targeted or striking naval mines, Iranian state media reported. Iran's Isl...
articles.full_text:
Seven oil tankers caught fire or were damaged in the Strait of Hormuz overnight into Thursday after being targeted or striking naval mines, Iranian state media reported.
Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps Navy, meanwhile, claimed that four of the vessels were involved in illegal oil transfers in the northern Persian Gulf. They were simultaneously hit and caught fire after being tracked by its forces Wednesday.
The IRGC added that three more vessels collided with mines west of the Strait of Hormuz.
The markedly high number of vessels affected in Hormuz, pointed to tensions winding upward over concerns about a return to all-out war.
With days before Israel’s close elections in which Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu could lose power and ahead of next month’s U.S. midterm elections in which war-linked high prices have sparked voter anger, there are concerns that U.S.-Israeli attacks on Iran could resume.
Iranian state television reported the claims about the latest attacks on ships, citing the Revolutionary Guard Corps navy, which again threatened to strike U.S. military bases in the region if the U.S. keeps helping to guide commercial ships through the strait.
The report did not mention casualties. A British military monitor, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations, did not report the attacks, but monitors in recent days have noted reluctance by some shippers to report incidents.
Iran still asserts control over the waterway, a central point of leverage in any talks with the U.S. over the war.
Iran’s top diplomat, Abbas Araghchi, on Wednesday said a wary Tehran remains open to diplomacy but is ready to defend itself.
Iran has warned that it has learned important military lessons from the war that began with U.S. and Israeli attacks on Feb. 28.
In recent days, Tehran has indicated it could expand targets to include infrastructure such as undersea cables and data centers.
The United States for its part is sending more military assets to the region, including a third aircraft carrier and thousands of troops, to join the largest force of American warships and aircraft in the Middle East in decades.
Mediators, meanwhile, have been trying to bring Washington and Tehran back to formal talks.
Iran is still promoting its latest proposal that would end the war and fully open the strait within a week if the U.S. meets several conditions. Those conditions, which include ending the U.S. blockade of Iranian ports, echo ones in the deal that fell apart within days of Washington and Tehran signing it in June.
U.S. President Donald Trump rejected that latest seven-day proposal, but both sides have acknowledged that indirect discussions have continued. Since that rejection, attacks on ships transiting the Strait of Hormuz have increased.
A return to all-out war would again endanger civilians throughout the region and complicate global deliveries of oil, natural gas and related products like fertilizer from the region and likely bring another spike in prices.

articles.title: QatarEnergy to purchase 4 million tons per year of US LNG from Cheniere through 2054 - Briefs Finance
articles.summary: QatarEnergy to purchase 4 million tons per year of US LNG from Cheniere through 2054  Briefs Finance
articles.full_text:
What happened
QatarEnergy signed a deal to source 4 million tons per year of LNG from Cheniere that extends to 2054, marking Qatar's first US offtake arrangement. The move comes as the company's own output has been constrained by the Iran war, which damaged the Ras Laffan facility and disrupted shipments, while traffic through the Strait of Hormuz has kept flows sharply reduced.
The agreement also signals a push to secure supply beyond the Middle East after the US overtook Qatar as the leading LNG exporter within a decade. Bloomberg News had previously reported that QatarEnergy was in talks with US suppliers for long-term volumes.
Deal details
QatarEnergy will lift 2 million tons per year from each of Cheniere's plants, Sabine Pass and Corpus Christi, with deliveries slated for the early 2030s and running through 2054, according to a statement Thursday. Of the Sabine Pass commitment, 1 million tons per year is contingent on a positive final investment decision for that facility's expansion phase.
President and CEO Saad Sherida Al-Kaabi said the two Cheniere agreements represented a key step in the company's LNG strategy. "This major long-term purchase will expand and diversify our global LNG portfolio and advance our ability to meet the evolving requirements of the market." He added, "The additional volumes will complement QatarEnergy's existing LNG supplies, enhance our supply and trading portfolio, and strengthen our ability to serve customers across the globe."

The broader context
Before the conflict, Qatar was among the largest LNG exporters. Damage at Ras Laffan during the war and continued shipping turmoil in the Strait of Hormuz have forced QatarEnergy to curtail output and deliveries, pushing the company to lock in supply elsewhere.
QatarEnergy already has US exposure through Golden Pass LNG in Texas, where it is the majority owner. The project, which includes ExxonMobil Holdings Corp. as a shareholder, is in startup and is planned to produce 18 million tons annually.
Why it matters for your portfolio
For LNG producers, long-term offtake deals are revenue anchors; for buyers, they are insurance against supply shocks. This contract secures decades of volumes for QatarEnergy while underscoring the US role in global LNG trade.
It also highlights a rebalancing in LNG supply chains as Qatar shores up non-Middle East sources during wartime disruptions. Watch knock-on effects for US exporters with expansion plans tied to final investment decisions and for shipping routes that can influence delivered costs.

articles.title: Iran says seven ships hit in Hormuz Strait, warns US of wider response - Al Jazeera
articles.summary: Iran says seven ships hit in Hormuz Strait, warns US of wider response  Al JazeeraIran says 7 oil tankers attacked in the Strait of Hormuz as fears grow of a return to war  YahooIran's IRGC Navy says seven vessels hit, warns US of wider response  ReutersOctober Marks Highest Number of Strait of Hormuz Attacks  USNI NewsSea mine crisis re-emerges in Strait of Hormuz as Tehran urges Washington to accept deal  Fox News
articles.full_text:
Iran says that seven oil tankers have been struck and sustained damage in the Strait of Hormuz, the largest single-day toll for the waterway since the United States and Israel started their war against Iran on February 28.
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said in a statement on Thursday that four of the vessels were transferring oil when they were targeted and caught fire overnight. The other three were disabled after striking mines.
The claims could not be independently verified, and the report did not provide details about possible casualties or the tankers’ flags.
The IRGC also warned that it could strike US bases across the Middle East if Washington moves to help tankers transit other parts of the strait.
“The US military must know that if this trend continues, the conflict will extend to its bases in the region,” the IRGC said in a statement on its Sepah News website. “This is a serious warning.”
Iran claims control over Hormuz, a strategic shipping route through which one-fifth of the world’s oil supplies passed before war broke out. It regularly attacks ships that attempt to navigate the strait without its authorisation.
But the US military has been escorting vessels through the waterway in increasing numbers, with Iran responding by stepping up attacks.
US President Donald Trump said on Thursday that “Iran is doing everything they can to drive up the price of oil prior to the US Midterm Election”.
In a post on his Truth Social platform, he added: “They are making up fake hits, mines, and everything else because more oil is coming through the Hormuz Strait now than it did even prior to the beginning of the conflict.”
A US Central Command spokesperson, speaking anonymously to Al Jazeera, also called Iran’s mine claims incorrect.
The spokesperson said US forces have cleared the international shipping lanes of mines and that Iran is using missiles and drones.
The strait remains open, the spokesperson said, with 95 percent of vessels getting through.
The attacks, the spokesperson added, show Tehran’s “desperation” under the US blockade, which cuts Iran off from the resources it needs to rebuild the military capabilities the US has said it destroyed.
Americans want ‘relief’ from war costs
“The number of ships and tankers attacked every single day is increasing, and Iran is saying it is continuing to do this because they are not going to allow any change in that situation,” said Al Jazeera’s Mohamed Vall, reporting from Tehran.
“They have full control over the Strait of Hormuz right now, they say.”
Vall said there is also talk in Tehran about an imminent escalation in the war, with the Iranians expecting the US to attack even before US midterm elections in early November.
“The IRGC army chief has boasted that Iran is more ready than anytime before, and has produced enough weapons and equipment to wage a symmetrical war against the United States,” he said.
Reporting from the US White House, Al Jazeera’s Kimberly Halkett said: “Striking Iran does not appear to serve any Republican interests”, adding that pre-election polls tell the same story for Trump’s political party.
“What we’ve seen in surveys in recent months, and as of today, is that most Americans want relief from their tax money going to pay for any potential war with Iran that is ramped up,” Halkett said.
“There is real frustration over the rising cost for everyday Americans, given the rising fuel prices that have occurred as a result of this conflict … As a result, the US president is having to make the case.
“The pressure is on the president, and it’s not just from the opposition party,” she said. “It is also from within the Republican Party as well.”

articles.title: 'Built on respect': EU gives International Criminal Court its top human rights prize as U.S. sanctions threaten to cut it off - Fortune
articles.summary: 'Built on respect': EU gives International Criminal Court its top human rights prize as U.S. sanctions threaten to cut it off  FortuneUS-sanctioned ICC wins Sakharov Prize, EU’s top human rights award  Al JazeeraInternational Criminal Court Wins E.U.’s Top Human Rights Prize  The New York TimesTrump-sanctioned ICC wins EU Parliament’s human rights prize  POLITICO.euEU Parliament awards Sakharov Prize to ICC in rebuke of US sanctions  Euronews
articles.full_text:
The International Criminal Court and its embattled staff have won the European Union’s top human rights honor, the Sakharov Prize, an official said Thursday.
The award came just days after the Trump administration announced sweeping new sanctions on the court, which is based in The Hague, Netherlands, as part of its campaign to dismantle the tribunal over investigations into the United States and its allies, including Israel.
“The European Union is built on respect for multilateralism and international institutions, and this prize recognizes the important work of the court in upholding international law and justice,” European Parliament President Roberta Metsola said.
Her announcement at the parliament in Strasbourg, France, was greeted with a standing ovation.
The annual EU award, named after Soviet dissident and Nobel Peace Prize laureate Andrei Sakharov, was created in 1988 to honor individuals or groups who defend human rights and basic freedoms.
A court under fire welcomes the award
ICC President Tomoko Akane of Japan welcomed the award, saying that it “comes at a time when the court and its officials face unprecedented challenges.”
“Against this backdrop, the Sakharov Prize carries particular significance, reaffirming the importance of independent judicial institutions and of those who work to uphold international law,” she said in a statement.
The ICC opened in 2002 as a court of last resort to prosecute senior leaders it deems responsible for crimes that, according to its founding treaty, “deeply shock the conscience of humanity.” It has jurisdiction over war crimes, crimes against humanity, genocide and the crime of aggression.
The Trump administration’s sanctions cut off the court from U.S.-based financial services, technology companies and even using U.S. dollars. They set a six-month timeline for U.S. companies and individuals that have business with the court to wind that business down.
The EU considers options to respond
In a statement after their summit last week, EU leaders said that the 27-nation bloc “deeply regrets” the Trump administration’s sanctions move and “urges the United States to reverse these latest measures.”
They noted that the U.S. has delayed the full impact of the sanctions by six months, and that “this creates space for diplomacy,” and expressed hope that the measures can ultimately be reversed.
Should diplomacy fail, however, the leaders insisted on “the EU’s readiness to take all necessary measures.”
They tasked the European Commission “to take all appropriate initiatives” to help protect the ICC and mitigate the impact of the sanctions, “specifically towards EU companies so that they can continue providing services to the Court.”
One possible retaliatory measure is the EU “blocking statute,” which could be used to protect European court staff, and possibly the Dutch-based court itself, by preventing European companies from complying with the U.S. measures.
An award for when rights and justice come under attack
The ICC and its officials were nominated for the prize by the Socialist and Democrats group in the European Parliament. The group, which unites center-left parties across Europe, said that it was “proud to have put forward their candidacy at a time when international justice is under attack.”
The Sakharov winner is chosen by the European Parliament’s president and top EU lawmakers from among candidates nominated by the parliament’s various political groups. The assembly says the award is “the highest tribute paid by the European Union to human rights work.”
Imprisoned Tanzanian opposition leader Tundu Lissu and Taraneh and Romina Rahimi — twins being held in prison for taking part in demonstrations against the Iranian government — were the others to make the EU shortlist.
Last year’s prize went to journalists Andrzej Poczobut and Mzia Amaghlobeli, who were imprisoned in Belarus and Georgia, respectively. Metsola said at the time that “their courage has made them symbols of the struggle for freedom and democracy.”
Several Sakharov laureates, including Nelson Mandela, Malala Yousafzai, Denis Mukwege and Nadia Murad, went on to win the Nobel Peace Prize. Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado, who won the Nobel Peace Prize last year, picked up the Sakharov Prize in 2024.
___
Mike Corder reported from The Hague, Netherlands.

articles.title: EU seeks stronger Qatar cooperation on security, trade and energy | Gulf Times - Gulf Times
articles.summary: EU seeks stronger Qatar cooperation on security, trade and energy | Gulf Times  Gulf Times
articles.full_text:
The European Union (EU) is seeking to turn its partnership with Qatar into practical co-operation across defence technology, artificial intelligence (AI), energy security, trade, and visa liberalisation, its ambassador to Doha has said.
Speaking to Gulf Times on the sidelines of the Global Security Forum, Antonino Maggiore said the two sides are working to translate their shared interests into concrete initiatives, with negotiations on a strategic partnership agreement providing a framework for closer engagement.
“We need to structure our co-operation,” he said. “We need to operationalise this co-operation because, as I said, it’s based on a convergence of principles. With principles, we need implementation.”
One forthcoming initiative is an EU-Gulf Co-operation Council (GCC) seminar on defence technology and AI, scheduled for Doha on December 3.
The event aims to bring defence industries from the EU’s 27 member states together with their Qatari counterparts and representatives from across the Gulf.
Maggiore said the EU could provide a platform for industries from its member states to interact with partners in Qatar and the wider region.
“These fields, security and defence and AI technology, are important in the partnership with Qatar,” he said, describing the seminar as part of efforts to develop cooperation in areas of growing strategic importance.
The initiative comes amid wider discussions on how Qatar and the EU can respond to changing security challenges, strengthen technological capabilities and establish practical channels for collaboration.
Asked about Qatar’s growing role in international diplomacy and mediation, Maggiore lauded the country’s contribution to efforts to address regional crises and other international issues.
“We commend, allow me to say, very, very much the prominent role of Qatar in mediation, also in the ongoing crisis in the region, but on so many other dossiers and so many other tables where Qatar is showing to be a global player of mediation and diplomacy,” he said.
He pointed to the Doha Forum in December as another opportunity to demonstrate Qatar’s diplomatic role, adding that the EU wanted to strengthen co-operation on mediation, maritime security, respect for international law and security.
The ambassador said the strategic partnership agreement under negotiation with Qatar would help organise co-operation across these areas, alongside separate initiatives designed to deliver tangible outcomes.
Economic engagement is another priority, particularly support for small- and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), investment and start-ups.
During a media Q&A session, Maggiore outlined plans for a business council that would bring together chambers of commerce from EU member states, corresponding Qatari entities, and European institutions.
A second component would build on the existing European Enterprise Network, which connects European businesses and SMEs and works with partners in non-EU countries.
“We want to support exchanges, investments, start-ups, youth,” he said. “Both big investments and also to SMEs. SMEs are cornerstones of the European Union.”
He said smaller businesses could benefit from structured support and connections that larger multinational companies often already have, adding that the EU saw considerable potential for closer economic ties with Qatar.
Trade is also part of the strategic partnership agreement discussions with Qatar and at the GCC level.
Energy remains central to the relationship.
Maggiore said he recently met Qatar’s minister of state for energy and stressed that dialogue on energy co-operation continues with the European Commission and EU member states.
He described Qatar’s liquefied natural gas (LNG) as being of “strategic importance for the EU”, adding that Brussels is fully aware of its significance.
Maggiore also praised Qatar’s engagement to maintain supplies and avoid unnecessary disruption, acknowledging the impact of the regional situation on production facilities.
“We are very pleased that Qatar is doing everything that is possible to maintain its engagement,” he said.
People-to-people ties and mobility are another area under discussion, the envoy said, with the EU working towards possible visa liberalisation for Qatari nationals.
Maggiore said the postponement of the EU-GCC summit, originally scheduled for October 24, would not affect the momentum of discussions on visas or the wider strategic partnership.
“The work is ongoing with, I would say, priority from our side,” he said, adding that meetings were taking place in Brussels with GCC countries and EU member states, which are responsible for issuing visas. “This is a priority for us, and it’s something we are working on very intensively.”
On the wider regional situation, Maggiore said that the Gulf and Europe shared concerns about instability and the threat of escalation.
He reiterated the EU’s support for dialogue, de-escalation, international law and a two-state solution to the Palestinian question.
The envoy also reaffirmed the EU’s opposition to illegal Israeli settlements in the West Bank.
He highlighted its humanitarian assistance to Palestine, while acknowledging that differences among member states could complicate the development of a common position.
Maggiore said the EU is ready to play a role in initiatives aimed at stabilisation, while recognising that other international actors also had a part to play.
He said the challenge for Qatar and the EU now is to build on political dialogue and shared interests by turning them into sustained co-operation across security, energy, business, and diplomacy.

articles.title: At least 4 Palestinians killed in Israeli attacks across Gaza
articles.summary: At least four Palestinians were killed and several others wounded Thursday in Israeli airstrikes and gunfire across the Gaza Strip, Palestinian medical officials said, as renewed a...
articles.full_text:
At least four Palestinians were killed and several others wounded Thursday in Israeli airstrikes and gunfire across the Gaza Strip, Palestinian medical officials said, as renewed attacks threatened to further undermine an already fragile cease-fire agreement.
The deaths were reported in separate incidents in Gaza City, Khan Younis, central Gaza and the northern Jabalia area, while Israeli forces continued shelling residential neighborhoods and areas sheltering displaced families.
In Gaza City, an Israeli drone struck a vehicle in the southwestern Tel al-Hawa neighborhood, killing at least one Palestinian and wounding others, including one person who sustained serious injuries, medical sources told Anadolu Agency.
The Interior Ministry said the attack killed a noncommissioned officer from its drug control police department and wounded another officer as they returned from an assignment.
Images from the scene showed emergency crews attempting to extinguish flames engulfing the vehicle as residents gathered nearby.
In the northern Gaza Strip, Israeli gunfire killed a Palestinian near the Jabalia refugee camp, according to medical sources. Initial reports differed on the victim's age, with one identifying the person as a girl and another as a woman.
In southern Gaza, an Israeli drone struck a motorcycle in Khan Younis, killing a Palestinian man and injuring two others, medical officials said.
Another Palestinian man was killed in a separate Israeli strike near the Nuseirat refugee camp in central Gaza, bringing the reported death toll from Thursday's attacks to at least four.
The Israeli military said it had targeted Hamas militants in Khan Younis, Nuseirat and Gaza City but was unaware of the reported shooting in Jabalia.
The military's account could not be independently reconciled with Palestinian reports of the casualties.
Israeli artillery fire also struck a school sheltering displaced Palestinians in Khan Younis, wounding four members of the same family, according to Palestinian medical and local sources.
A medical source at Nasser Hospital said a man, his wife and their two children were admitted with injuries of varying severity after a shell hit a tent in the courtyard of Mustafa Hafez School.
The school had been serving as a shelter for Palestinians displaced by the prolonged Israeli military offensive.
Witnesses also reported heavy gunfire from Israeli military vehicles targeting areas near residential buildings and tents housing displaced families east of Hamad City in Khan Younis.
In Gaza City, Israeli forces carried out additional attacks on residential properties early Thursday.
Witnesses said an Israeli helicopter struck an evacuated apartment in the Rimal neighborhood, while a drone targeted an empty house in the Nasr neighborhood that had already sustained damage in previous Israeli bombardment.
Israeli forces also continued demolishing residential buildings in the eastern Tuffah and Shujaiya neighborhoods.
Residents reported hearing two powerful explosions overnight and early Thursday as demolition operations continued.
Israeli artillery also shelled areas near the Al-Sanafour junction east of Tuffah, accompanied by heavy gunfire from military vehicles positioned nearby.
The latest attacks come amid growing tensions over the implementation of the U.S.-brokered cease-fire agreement that took effect on Oct. 10, 2025.
Palestinian authorities have repeatedly accused Israel of violating the agreement through continued airstrikes, artillery attacks and gunfire across the enclave.
According to figures reported by Palestinian authorities as of Wednesday, Israeli attacks since the cease-fire began had killed 1,538 Palestinians and wounded 5,498 others.
Israel, meanwhile, has accused Hamas of attempting to rebuild its military capabilities and carrying out attacks in violation of the agreement.
Hamas has denied the accusations, rejecting claims that it has sought to launch new attacks or rearm, and has accused Israel of undermining the cease-fire through continued military operations.
The Israeli military has intensified strikes in recent weeks, further raising concerns about the durability of the truce.
Israeli authorities say four Israeli soldiers have been killed since the cease-fire took effect.
Although the agreement was intended to pave the way for the eventual reconstruction of Gaza, negotiations over key provisions have made little progress.
Disagreements over the disarmament of Hamas and the withdrawal of Israeli forces from the territory have prevented the sides from reaching a comprehensive arrangement for the next stages of the agreement.
The continued hostilities have also complicated efforts to restore essential services and rebuild civilian infrastructure devastated during more than three years of war.
Since October 2023, Israeli military operations have killed more than 74,000 Palestinians and wounded over 175,000 others in Gaza, according to Palestinian authorities.
Local authorities estimate that approximately 90% of the enclave's civilian infrastructure has been destroyed or damaged during the offensive.
Israel launched its military campaign following the Hamas-led attacks on southern Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, which killed approximately 1,200 people, according to Israeli figures.
Despite the cease-fire, recurring Israeli attacks and the lack of progress on unresolved political and security issues continue to leave Gaza's population facing widespread displacement, destruction and uncertainty.

articles.title: Israeli settler violence in West Bank spiraling out of control: UN
articles.summary: U.N. Secretary-General Antonio Guterres warned Thursday that escalating violence in the Israeli-occupied West Bank has spiraled out of control, with mounting attacks by Israeli set...
articles.full_text:
U.N. Secretary-General Antonio Guterres warned Thursday that escalating violence in the Israeli-occupied West Bank has spiraled out of control, with mounting attacks by Israeli settler terrorists threatening to forcibly displace Palestinian communities from their land.
"In the occupied West Bank, Palestinians continue to suffer daily attacks by Israeli settlers. The clear goal is to drive communities off their land," Guterres told reporters.
He said the situation in the occupied territories is "simply out of control" as Israeli illegal settlers also target journalists and diplomats.
On Gaza, the U.N. chief pointed out that essential humanitarian assistance remains "severely restricted" ahead of winter, compounding obstacles facing the Security Council-backed roadmap to resolve the conflict.
Guterres stressed that the World Food Program "urgently" requires $450 million to feed populations across Gaza and the West Bank over the next six months, noting that the sum equals approximately 90 minutes of global military expenditures. He appealed to international donors to step up while urging an end to the occupation to achieve a viable two-state solution.
Guterres compared modern conflicts to the climate phenomenon El Nino, and cautioned that cascading hostilities are reverberating through international energy markets, shipping corridors, and financial systems.
He linked widespread street protests over inflation, food, and fuel directly to the fallout of expanding global wars. "War does not create all these inequalities, but it feeds and exploits them," Guterres said, emphasizing that while street violence is unacceptable, authorities cannot allow disorder to obscure the legitimate cost-of-living grievances of peaceful protesters.
Guterres also dismissed concerns about institutional damage to the UN from violations of international law, declaring that the real crisis is the suffering of ordinary civilians whose survival is threatened by war-induced inflation and violence.
"The problem is not for the United Nations. The problem is for the people that is suffering dramatically everywhere," he said.

articles.title: Rubio, Qatar PM discuss Mideast tensions, Hormuz navigation
articles.summary: U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani discussed efforts to ease escalating Middle East tensions and safeguard marit...
articles.full_text:
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani discussed efforts to ease escalating Middle East tensions and safeguard maritime navigation through the strategic Strait of Hormuz during a phone call Thursday, as diplomatic efforts continue to prevent further regional instability.
Rubio expressed appreciation for Qatar's ongoing mediation efforts in the region and reaffirmed Washington's commitment to the Gulf nation's security and freedom of navigation through the vital waterway, according to a statement from the U.S. State Department.
Qatar's Foreign Ministry said the two officials, with Sheikh Mohammed also serving as foreign minister, reviewed the latest regional developments and discussed ways to strengthen the strategic partnership between Doha and Washington.
Their talks focused on ongoing diplomatic initiatives and joint coordination aimed at reducing tensions, enhancing regional security and promoting stability across the Middle East.
Sheikh Mohammed reiterated Qatar's support for diplomatic efforts to reach a settlement that would guarantee freedom of maritime navigation and pave the way for a comprehensive agreement capable of securing lasting regional peace, the ministry said.
The discussions come amid persistent tensions surrounding the Strait of Hormuz, one of the world's most strategically important maritime corridors and a crucial transit route for global oil and liquefied natural gas shipments.
Washington and Tehran remain divided over navigation rights in the waterway, with Iran asserting its authority to regulate passage through the strait while the United States insists on unrestricted maritime access.
The dispute has heightened concerns over regional security and the potential consequences of disruptions to international energy supplies.
Qatar, which maintains diplomatic channels with both Washington and Tehran, has played an active role in mediation efforts aimed at reducing tensions and facilitating negotiations between the two sides.
Thursday's call underscored the importance both countries attach to continued diplomatic engagement as efforts intensify to prevent further escalation and secure a negotiated resolution to regional disputes.

articles.title: Thieving Israeli settlers hit Palestinian olive harvest hard in W. Bank
articles.summary: Spike in violence and widespread theft by terrorist settlers have plagued the West Bank olive harvest this year, a trend Palestinian residents, Israeli human rights groups and the...
articles.full_text:
Spike in violence and widespread theft by terrorist settlers have plagued the West Bank olive harvest this year, a trend Palestinian residents, Israeli human rights groups and the U.N. say follows decades of intimidation.
Brought to tears as he recalled Israeli settlers hitting his cherished olive trees with sticks and taking off with the olives, Palestinian Ahmed Salem said he feared being attacked if he tried to intervene.
The Jewish settlers dumped Salem's olives into sacks and then drove them to a nearby Israeli settler outpost to be pressed into olive oil, the 50-year-old Palestinian told Reuters of the incident around two weeks ago near his village Lubban al-Gharbi.
"How would you feel if something that belonged to you was being violated and you could do nothing about it?" he asked.
The couple living in the outpost, whose olive press settlers have urged Israelis to use for West Bank olives, declined multiple Reuters requests for comment, while the Yesha Council, which oversees Israeli settlements in the West Bank, did not immediately respond.
The attacks have accelerated ahead of an Israeli election next week that opinion polls show Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his pro-settler coalition could lose to opponents who have taken a more critical stance against settler violence.
The olive harvest starts with the onset of cooler weather, allowing Palestinian families to gather in the lush, terraced groves that they have groomed for generations.
"My 6-year-old son remembers going there with me, eating there, making tea there," Salem said.
With the establishment of hundreds of small settler outposts under Netanyahu's government since 2022, the military has increasingly restricted Palestinian access to areas nearby, including many olive groves.
"This creates a situation where Palestinians, in many of the cases, many of the lands, especially in proximity to settlements and outposts, cannot enter the land and harvest the trees," said Ziv Stahl, executive director of Israeli rights group Yesh Din.
"But settlers can come and go freely and that's what they do."
Even when Palestinians can access their trees, it is not without risk. Yesh Din on Wednesday reported 125 physical attacks on Palestinian olive harvesters over the 24 days since the season began and 168 incidents of crop theft, with Israeli military forces present in at least a quarter of cases.
An Israeli military official said it takes acts of violence, criminal activity and attempts to undermine security very seriously. The official did not refer to settlers or comment on the reports of olive theft in the presence of the Israeli military, which has separately uprooted trees with excavators, citing what it said was a need to prevent Palestinian attacks.
The removal of Palestinians' olives has met with widely differing responses from Israeli rabbis.
"I call it theft. From my perspective, I define it as theft or robbery and it is forbidden," said Zev Weitman, the rabbi for the Alon Shvut settlement south of Bethlehem.
Prominent Orthodox rabbi Dov Lior said settlers should harvest across the West Bank, asserting in an open letter that Palestinians had no ownership rights to the land and that harvesting olives fulfilled "the commandment of conquering the land."
Hundreds of acres of the land around Salem's village, Lubban al-Gharbi, including olive groves, were fenced off and seized between 2023 and 2026 by Avichai Farm, an Israeli settler outpost built on a nearby hill.
Salem said villagers have seen settlers harvest olives from the seized land and take them to the outpost's olive press.
At the start of the olive harvest, settlers posted on social media calling on Israelis to harvest occupied West Bank olives and bring them to Avichai Farm's press.
"Both fine oil and strengthening the Jewish hold on the vast expanses of our land!," read a message on a settler Telegram group. "It's either us or our enemy!"
The press at Avichai Farm advertises "premium products produced by Avichai Farm" with olive oil at about $20 a bottle via a website run by the Farms Association, a settler group that Reuters has reported receives significant financial support from the Israeli government, which says the aim is to promote peace.
The Farms Association did not immediately respond to a request for comment and the couple who live on the farm with their children declined to be interviewed by a Reuters reporter who approached the area Sunday.
On a road leading to Avichai Farm, Reuters spoke to a man who declined to be identified and said he had driven from a settlement around 90 minutes away to press 14 bags of olives from trees he said he grew himself.
Lubban al-Gharbi villagers and other Palestinians who have lost land to settler expansion say the harvesting of olives from trees in groves seized from Palestinian land constitutes theft.
U.N. bodies and most countries deem Israel's settlements on land occupied in war illegal under international law regarding military occupations. Israel rejects this, viewing the territory as disputed rather than occupied.
During this year's olive harvest, Palestinian authorities say three Palestinians have been killed in daily settler terrorist attacks, which have also injured several journalists, European diplomats and a French mayor.
Stahl from the Yesh Din Israeli rights group said the violence was "part of a campaign of ethnic cleansing, paving the way for the annexation of the West Bank without its Palestinian population."
Israel, which has considered the idea of annexation, said it is investigating some of the incidents.
An Israeli government spokesperson said olives "picked by a Jew in the ancestral homeland of the Jewish people" did not constitute theft and that Jews owned and cultivated "millions of olive trees" in the area. No one should take the law into their own hands, the spokesperson added.
Palestinian farmer Samer Ben Shamsi said masked settlers attacked him on Oct. 9 in the Palestinian village of Beita near Nablus, then sped away in a pickup truck with his harvest of olives after he and other farmers fled.
"This year, they steal without fear because they have a state and a powerful force backing them," Ben Shamsi said, referring to the security forces.
Within the past year alone, settlers had shot him in the leg, beaten him and smashed his possessions, he said.
"We pay in blood for the olives."

articles.title: Israeli troops kill disabled civilian, abduct youth in S. Syria
articles.summary: Israeli forces killed a disabled civilian in Daraa province and abducted a young man while blocking a U.N. patrol in neighboring Quneitra province Thursday, according to local medi...
articles.full_text:
Israeli forces killed a disabled civilian in Daraa province and abducted a young man while blocking a U.N. patrol in neighboring Quneitra province Thursday, according to local media.
Alikhbariah TV reported that Israeli forces entered Taranja village in northern Quneitra countryside with seven military vehicles and abducted a young man.
They also obstructed the passage of a patrol belonging to the U.N. Disengagement Observer Force (UNDOF) by blocking the village road.
The broadcaster did not provide details about the young man’s identity or where he was taken.
Earlier Thursday, Israeli forces entered Jamlah village in western Daraa province and shot dead a civilian with disabilities, according to Syria’s official SANA news agency.
The victim’s body was transferred to Daraa National Hospital. The agency did not identify him or specify the nature of his disability.
During the incursion into Jamlah, Israeli forces deployed in the village’s eastern neighborhood and positioned snipers on the rooftops of residential buildings, SANA reported.
Alikhbariah TV also said Israeli troops searched several houses and fired indiscriminately in residential neighborhoods.
On Wednesday evening, Israeli artillery shelled the outskirts of Abidin village in the Yarmouk Basin area of western Daraa.
SANA reported that two shells landed west of the village, with no information available on casualties or material damage.
On Sunday, Syria’s Foreign Ministry condemned escalating Israeli incursions into Quneitra province and the Daraa countryside, alongside increased helicopter, reconnaissance and warplane flights over southern Syria.
The ministry warned that continued violations "undermine the prospects for achieving stability and security in the region in general and Syria in particular, and obstruct reconstruction and recovery efforts."
It called on the international community to put an end to the violations and compel Israel to comply with international law and relevant U.N. resolutions.
Israel has occupied most of Syria’s Golan Heights since 1967. Following the fall of Bashar Assad’s regime, Israeli forces seized the demilitarized buffer zone and expanded their presence in southern Syria.
The 1974 disengagement agreement established a U.N.-monitored buffer zone between Syrian and Israeli forces.
Syria and Israel have held several rounds of U.S.-mediated talks aimed at reducing tensions, halting Israeli military operations, and reaching a security agreement.
In August, Syrian and Israeli delegations met in Jordan under U.S. mediation to discuss measures to halt Israeli attacks, arrests and military operations, as well as the withdrawal of Israeli forces to positions held before December 2024.

articles.title: 7 dead as Russia-Ukraine trade strikes despite diplomatic overtures
articles.summary: Russia and Ukraine traded overnight attacks that left seven dead on the Ukrainian side, authorities said Thursday, shortly after U.S. President Donald Trump's envoy met with Russia...
articles.full_text:
Russia and Ukraine traded overnight attacks that left seven dead on the Ukrainian side, authorities said Thursday, shortly after U.S. President Donald Trump's envoy met with Russian President Vladimir Putin in St. Petersburg.
Trump struck an optimistic tone after his envoy Steve Witkoff's meeting with Putin Wednesday, saying negotiators were "maybe now the closest we've been" to ending the war.
The Kremlin said it was open "in principle" to resuming trilateral talks involving the two sides and the United States.
But attacks did not cease after the visit.
Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said two people were wounded in barrages of 630 drones fired at the region, with 163 approaching the capital.
The governor of the nearby Tula region said Russian air defenses destroyed 70 drones. Another man was wounded in the Lipetsk region, its governor said.
In Ukraine, the attacks killed one man in Sumy and a woman in Kharkiv, both in the northeast, as well as three people in southeastern Zaporizhzhia and two in the eastern Donetsk region, authorities said.
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said on social media strikes wounded 15 people in the capital.
He said the strikes damaged metro infrastructure at the Pivdenny Bridge, which officials said restricted traffic between parts of the city.
Ukraine's air force warned in the early hours of "more ballistic missiles toward Kyiv" and instructed residents to stay in shelters.
Witkoff flew to Russia from a meeting with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Oslo Tuesday, aimed at smoothing a bitter rift between Trump and the Ukrainian leader.
Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner also took part in the talks with Putin remotely.
Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov told reporters Russia was "in principle" ready to resume trilateral talks in mid-November – after the U.S. midterm elections – and that the Kremlin wanted them to focus on postwar security.
Zelenskyy said Ukraine also backed resuming trilateral talks.
Ushakov said Witkoff briefed Putin on "some new aspects in the approaches of the Europeans and Kyiv" from the Oslo meeting but added that "there wasn't really much substance in them."
Ushakov also said a summit between Putin, U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping was in preparation in Shenzhen, China, for next month, calling it "the first such meeting in history."
During their three-hour meeting, Witkoff praised Putin for granting Trump's request to free U.S. citizen Stephen Hubbard, a retired English teacher in his 70s who was detained for fighting for Ukraine – charges he denied.
"You talk so much about my president, President Trump, being a humanitarian – you are a humanitarian also, sir, and I salute that," Witkoff said.
Witkoff said on social media the talks with Putin were "constructive," adding that "there is still important work left to do." Discussions would continue between the United States, Ukraine and Russia at the technical level, he added.
U.S. President Donald Trump returned to power in January 2025 promising to end the war in 24 hours – but more than a year of U.S.-led talks have failed to produce a breakthrough.
In recent days, a frustrated Trump once again pivoted away from Ukraine and back to Putin, touting what he called a deal for Russia to sell diesel and reduce prices sent soaring by the Iran war.
Trump also delayed the imposition of sanctions on Russia's war effort – a decision he defended Wednesday as necessary to secure Hubbard's release.
"If you had put those sanctions on ... you could forget about him; you'd never see him again," Trump told reporters at the White House.
Witkoff told Putin Washington was "grateful" for the diesel deal, which sparked outrage in Kyiv and across Europe.
The war, Europe's worst since World War II, has killed tens of thousands of people since Russia's February 2022 invasion.
Putin has consistently rejected face-to-face talks with Zelenskyy and insisted Moscow intends to seize the rest of eastern Ukraine.

articles.title: Ilhan Omar says moving out of Washington home after federal search
articles.summary: U.S. Rep. Ilhan Omar said Wednesday she will move out of her Washington, D.C., home that federal agents searched last week, noting that attention brought on by the raid has made he...
articles.full_text:
U.S. Rep. Ilhan Omar said Wednesday she will move out of her Washington, D.C., home that federal agents searched last week, noting that attention brought on by the raid has made her feel unsafe there.
Federal authorities are investigating alleged fraud in her family's immigration paperwork and have issued grand jury subpoenas to some of her relatives, a person briefed on the investigation told The Associated Press (AP) on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to discuss an ongoing investigation.
Omar, who was born in Somalia and is a naturalized U.S. citizen, condemned the raid as politically motivated. The search also drew swift condemnation from Democrats.
In her first interview since the search, she said on Wednesday she is "confident in the fact that I didn't do anything wrong."
The progressive Minnesota Democrat has been a frequent critic and target of President Donald Trump, who has on multiple occasions pushed for the prosecution of his perceived political enemies.
Referring to her roots, Trump has several times suggested that Omar should "go back" to Somalia.
In the interview with MS NOW, Omar said she was rattled by the search weeks out from the Nov. 3 midterms, which will decide control of the House and Senate. She is running for reelection in a deep blue district centered in Minneapolis and is expected to retain her seat.
Omar recalled waking around 6 a.m. to Homeland Security investigators banging on her door with a warrant. They searched for four or five hours and seized 17 items, including phones, notebooks, a Somali language children's book and a vintage camera that her husband had received as a gift, she said.
The Justice Department has shared few details about the case other than saying it was a criminal investigation.
Omar came with her family to the U.S. at age 12, after they obtained asylum. She became a U.S. citizen five years later, in 2000.
"It would be a huge undertaking to, I suppose, indict a 12-year-old for so cleverly conspiring to defraud immigration services to come to the United States. I'm sure there are a lot of smart 12-year-olds, but that seems like a leap," she said in the interview.
Congressional Democrats also questioned the timing. The Justice Department has historically avoided overt investigative actions involving candidates in the immediate run-up to an election.
Omar said the agents were "intrusive but polite," logging the items they took and putting back everything else in its place.

articles.title: Trump's Pentagon breaks world? Just historic globe
articles.summary: Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth asked aides to retrieve a globe linked to legendary World War II General Dwight Eisenhower, only for them to break it, a report said Thursday. The large...
articles.full_text:
Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth asked aides to retrieve a globe linked to legendary World War II General Dwight Eisenhower, only for them to break it, a report said Thursday.
The large orb fell while being carried by untrained staff, resulting in the loss of a large chunk of the world near Antarctica, The Washington Post said.
The Post reported that historic items are typically moved around the Pentagon premises by trained curators. However, Hegseth's office had dispatched its own team.
Photographs published by the Post showed the hole in the Antarctica area and an accompanying plaque identifying it as one of two nearly identical, historic "Eisenhower Globes" in the Pentagon's possession.
The Army acknowledged the damage in a statement to the Post. Army spokesperson Christopher Surridge said the globe was damaged during an "attempted move" on Feb. 3. Aside from the hole, "the spherical portion of the globe was detached from the metal mounting that allows it to rotate," Surridge was quoted.
After the report, a Defense Department official provided the Post with a brief, unattributed statement acknowledging the mishap.
"Accidents happen," it said. "We are grateful no one was harmed, and the globe is being repaired."
President Donald Trump's secretary of defense has focused on promoting a muscular image for the U.S. military, starting by attempting to restore the Department of War name, which was dropped in 1947 for the Department of Defense.
Hegseth, who rose as far as major during an Army National Guard career before becoming a Fox News host, regularly does televised exercise routines with troops. He has ordered mandatory testosterone screening for male military staff over 30.
He is currently overseeing the eight-month war against Iran, which Trump has promised repeatedly to bring to a rapid conclusion.
Eisenhower led the U.S. war effort against Nazi Germany, commanding the D-Day landings that launched the phase of conflict leading to Adolf Hitler's defeat.
A five-star general, he was then elected president in 1952, taking the helm of the White House as the Cold War gathered pace. He was often photographed posing alongside elaborate globes.

articles.title: Thousands of student movement supporters rally as Serbia heads to poll
articles.summary: Tens of thousands of supporters of Serbia's opposition student movement gathered in central Belgrade on Thursday, as the country's longtime leader Aleksandar Vucic rallied across t...
articles.full_text:
Tens of thousands of supporters of Serbia's opposition student movement gathered in central Belgrade on Thursday, as the country's longtime leader Aleksandar Vucic rallied across town at the dueling final events ahead of pivotal parliamentary elections.
The Student List, a leaderless movement of student-backed candidates, is seeking to end more than 14 years of rule by Vucic's right-wing populist Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) when the country votes on Sunday.
It is the biggest threat Vucic has faced to his hold on power, and civil society groups have warned the election campaign has been marred by intimidation, arrests, attacks, misuse of public resources and a distorted media environment.
"I came to support the Student List because young people finally gave me hope that it is possible to live in a normal country," 47-year-old Marija Nedeljkovic Radic told Agence France-Presse (AFP) as she arrived for the students' rally.
"Really, for the first time in my life, I believe that it is possible."
The vote comes after nearly two years of student-led protests sparked by the 2024 collapse of a canopy at the newly renovated Novi Sad railway station that killed 16 people.
The tragedy, widely blamed on corruption, triggered some of Serbia's largest protests since the fall of Slobodan Milosevic, accused architect of genocide in the Balkans, in 2000.
The anti-corruption movement, led by university students, snowballed from demands for a transparent investigation into the tragedy into calls for an early election.
Waving "Students are winning" flags, chanting and blowing whistles, students marched through Belgrade before converging on Slavija Square, the site of some of their biggest protests.
By early evening, thousands had arrived, and crowds were still growing.
Vucic has dominated Serbian politics for over a decade, serving as either prime minister or president.
Amid mounting pressure, he announced the snap vote last month, setting up his biggest electoral challenge since his party took power in 2012.
Vucic, who addressed supporters at a sports hall in the capital on Thursday, has regularly accused the student movement of being a foreign-funded coup attempt.
"Let us never forget how they tried to bring down our state. Let us always protect and defend it," said the 56-year-old, who resigned to run for prime minister.
"Let us go out and defeat them! Defeat them decisively!" he said before white ticker tape and balloons showered the crowd.
Many of the 250 candidates of the Student List running for the 250-seat parliament are drawn from academia or are deliberate political outsiders.
The movement has a broad platform, but at its core is a pledge to fight corruption.
Serbia lacks reliable independent polling, and surveys have produced widely differing results.
Political scientist Dusan Vucicevic from Belgrade University told AFP it was difficult to predict an outcome but expected students to win more than 40% of the vote, a result significantly larger than any opposition list since SNS came to power.
Days before the vote, Serbian civil society groups warned that conditions for "free and fair elections" were lacking.
"This assessment is not based on isolated incidents, opposition claims or political disagreement with the government," a joint statement by 24 organizations said.
"It is supported by documented findings from independent Serbian organizations working in different fields."
On Wednesday, Belgrade prosecutors questioned six people arrested on suspicion of plotting "violence, riots and attacks" on election day.
Reports of threats and intimidation targeting student demonstrators have grown in recent months, but their rallies have remained largely peaceful since they began.
"I've been following this fight since the very beginning," 35-year-old student rally attendee Igor said.
"Today is the last rally, and it's important that we all come here to send a message of love and peace and that we see each other on the 25th at the polling stations."

articles.title: Powerful magnitude 7.0 earthquake strikes China's Tibet region
articles.summary: A powerful magnitude 7.0 earthquake struck southwestern China's Tibet region late Thursday, the China Earthquake Networks Center (CENC) reported, with the tremor recorded at 10:33...
articles.full_text:
A powerful magnitude 7.0 earthquake struck southwestern China's Tibet region late Thursday, the China Earthquake Networks Center (CENC) reported, with the tremor recorded at 10:33 p.m. local time (2:33 p.m. GMT).
Local authorities have found at least two people injured in a village near the epicentre, with some houses in villages closest to the epicenter showing cracks, the state broadcaster said. The quake is the strongest to hit China since January 2024.
The epicenter was in a sparsely populated, high-altitude county in Nagqu, northern Tibet, at a depth of 10 km (6.2 miles). The average elevation within 5 km of the epicenter is about 4,864 meters (15,960 feet), CENC data showed.
Videos released by local officially run media showed people leaving their homes and seeking shelter outside or in their cars parked on the street. One resident reported being awakened by the strong quake and heard the house squeaking in the tremor.
The quake was clearly felt in the local area, CENC said. The epicenter was around 400 km from the Tibetan capital of Lhasa.
Local fire and rescue teams have mobilized and are heading to the affected region, state media said.
A string of smaller tremors of around magnitude 3 and 4 have been recorded in surrounding regions following the magnitude 7 quake, CENC data showed.
In 2010, a magnitude 7.1 tremor struck Yushu in neighboring Qinghai province, killing at least 2,698 people and leaving nearly 300 people missing.

articles.title: Finland licenses world's first permanent nuclear waste repository
articles.summary: Finland has approved the operation of the world's first permanent underground repository for spent nuclear fuel, marking a major milestone in radioactive waste management more than...
articles.full_text:
Finland has approved the operation of the world's first permanent underground repository for spent nuclear fuel, marking a major milestone in radioactive waste management more than two decades after construction began, operator Posiva said Thursday.
Blasted into 1.9 billion-year-old stable bedrock in Eurajoki in southwestern Finland, the geological repository will house spent nuclear fuel in holes drilled into the bedrock, where it will remain harmfully radioactive for thousands of years.
"This is a great and historic day for both Posiva and Finland," Posiva chief executive Ilkka Poikolainen said in a statement.
The site, dubbed Onkalo, which means "cave" in Finnish, is expected to start operations soon, but Posiva said no exact date had been decided yet.
"No detailed schedule is given at this point for the start-up," it said.
"Before final disposal begins, Posiva will finalize the commissioning stage, carrying out the necessary tests and inspections which STUK (the Finnish Radiation and Nuclear Safety Authority) also needs to verify and approve."
With space for 6,500 tons of uranium, Onkalo will provide permanent storage for spent fuel from Finland's five nuclear reactors.
The fuel will be encapsulated in copper canisters that are highly resistant to corrosion, then lowered into holes drilled in tunnels in the bedrock, which will be filled with bentonite clay and finally sealed with a steel-reinforced concrete plug.
The fuel will be highly radioactive for tens of thousands of years. After about 100,000 years, the levels will be about the same as the uranium ore of which the fuel is made, according to Posiva.
Countries have been wrestling with what to do with dangerous nuclear by-products since the first plants were built in the 1950s. Currently, most of it is in temporary storage.
Final repositories are being built in other countries, including neighbouring Sweden and in France, but Finland is expected to be first to open its underground storage facility.
The cost of the Onkalo site has been estimated at $1.16 billion.

articles.title: ICC wins top EU human rights honor while in Trump's crosshairs
articles.summary: The EU awarded its top human rights prize to the International Criminal Court Thursday, defying U.S. President Donald Trump, who recently hit the war crimes tribunal with sweeping...
articles.full_text:
The EU awarded its top human rights prize to the International Criminal Court Thursday, defying U.S. President Donald Trump, who recently hit the war crimes tribunal with sweeping sanctions.
"The European Union is built on respect for multilateralism and international institutions and this prize recognizes the important work of the court in upholding international law and justice," said Roberta Metsola, chief of the European Parliament, announcing the award.
The ICC thanked the European Parliament for giving it the Sakharov Prize "at a time when the court and its officials face unprecedented challenges."
"Against this backdrop, the Sakharov Prize carries particular significance, reaffirming the importance of independent judicial institutions and of those who work to uphold international law," said Tomoko Akane, president of the ICC.
This month, the United States announced sanctions against the ICC aimed at crippling the day-to-day operations of the court, which prosecutes individuals for war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide.
U.S. President Donald Trump's administration has vowed to dismantle the court "brick by brick," furious that judges have issued an arrest warrant for Benjamin Netanyahu, Israel's prime minister, for war crimes in Gaza.
The win comes after former ICC judge Navi Pillay, who also served as U.N. human rights chief, received the Nobel Peace Prize this month. U.S. President Donald Trump slammed the choice as "disgraceful," arguing the award should have gone to him.
The EU has already thrown its support behind the ICC in the face of U.S. sanctions, which will come into force in six months and has said it is "ready to take any necessary measures" to make sure the court can continue working.
"The International Criminal Court must be free to pursue its mission independently and without pressure or intimidation," said Ursula von der Leyen, chief of the EU, after the prize was announced.
Brussels hopes to use the delay before the sanctions are applied to try to persuade the U.S. to reconsider, but it is also considering implementing a "blocking statute" to shield the ICC from Washington.
Established in 1988 and named after Soviet dissident Andrei Sakharov, the EU prize is bestowed annually on individuals or organizations to recognize their fight for human rights and democracy.
The ICC was among three finalists this year, alongside Tundu Lissu, a Tanzanian opposition leader, and twin sisters Taraneh and Romina Rahimi, who represent those prosecuted by the Iranian government.
The nominees are nominated by the political groups in the EU, and the winner is chosen by senior lawmakers. An award ceremony will be held in December.
Lissu, head of Tanzania's opposition Chadema party, was detained on April 9, 2025. He faces a possible death penalty if convicted of treason for allegedly inciting the public to boycott elections last year.
Taraneh and Romina Rahimi, 21, have been sentenced, respectively, to death and 36 years in prison for taking part in anti-government protests in Iran.
Other recent high-profile winners of the Sakharov Prize have been Maria Corina Machado, a Venezuelan opposition chief; the late Russian Kremlin critic Alexei Navalny and the people of Ukraine.

articles.title: Macron slams ‘stupid’ claims blaming Muslims for France unrest
articles.summary: French President Emmanuel Macron said Wednesday that foreign leaders, including those "on the other side of the Atlantic," are attempting to exploit recent street violence and loot...
articles.full_text:
French President Emmanuel Macron said Wednesday that foreign leaders, including those "on the other side of the Atlantic," are attempting to exploit recent street violence and looting in France for political gain.
Protests over soaring living costs have led to widespread rioting and looting that have drawn worldwide attention and shocked many French citizens.
U.S. President Donald Trump has used the violence to rally his political supporters, making unsubstantiated claims that Muslim migrants are responsible for the unrest and urging Macron to "close your borders and take control before it is too late!"
Macron responded by saying there "has been foreign manipulation of information in the aftermath" of the looting in Paris and other French cities last weekend. "And that has led to comments that are as unacceptable as they are stupid, from many people, including foreign leaders," he said.
Asked by a reporter if he was referring to Trump, Macron replied: "Among others." He added that there have been "AI-generated images depicting scenes that never actually happened in France. We've had people claiming that we were invaded by hordes of migrants and Islamists, which is completely false."
Macron did not specify which AI-generated images he was referring to, nor how he knew the content was false.
French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said his office can provide the countries concerned with the necessary clarification, "to help them avoid spreading or amplifying false information and making baseless claims on social media."
Macron and Trump once enjoyed a good relationship but Trump regularly mocks the French president in his public speeches.
"The fact is, all the people who are speaking ill of our country right now are people who don't love our country," Macron said. "So those people really bother me."
"When I see leaders who are in the middle of election campaigns, whether in the region or on the other side of the Atlantic – who sometimes naively repeat AI-generated content or spread narratives that certain circles are clearly trying to promote about what happened in France – they're using our country for their own political campaigns," said Macron. "And we don't need that."
Macron was speaking in Qatar at the end of a tour of key energy suppliers in Gulf Arab states, where he secured an additional 100,000 metric tons of diesel per month from the United Arab Emirates, with a further 100,000 tons to be confirmed in Bahrain.
Macron's office said he traveled to the Middle East to find solutions to the energy crisis and rising energy prices, and to secure supplies of oil, gas, diesel and jet fuel.
The Elysee said nearly 295,000 additional tons of diesel per month could be secured, including supplies from Saudi Arabia – equivalent to more than 10% of France's monthly diesel consumption.
Macron later traveled to Saudi Arabia to meet Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman "to continue efforts to secure and diversify oil and gas supplies," according to his office.
Earlier this month, the Group of Seven (G-7) wealthy democracies agreed to release 100 million barrels of oil and fuel products, beginning with substantial quantities of diesel after the fuel's price hit a record high in the United States.
"I would remind you that France initiated the G-7 meeting that led to the release of strategic reserves, which, through implementation at the national level, will help bring down prices starting in early November," Macron said.
Petrol, energy and food prices have surged in recent months, and it remains to be seen whether Macron's announcement will ease protesters' anger. He said the additional diesel supplies addressed "some of the anxieties."
"I also hear the concerns of our high school and university students. Those concerns stem from other factors, but in any case, I think things are moving in the right direction," he added.
High school students have raised concerns about underfunded schools, dilapidated facilities and staff shortages, particularly in lower-income neighborhoods.
Some also say school days, which often run from 8 a.m. to 6 p.m., are exhausting and the university admissions system is complex and unfair.
France has had two consecutive quiet nights since the weekend's unrest. Curfews have been imposed in parts of several major cities, including small areas of Paris.
Further protests are planned for Thursday and Saturday following calls from student unions and groups within the "Yellow Vest" movement, whose demonstrations over fuel prices shook France in 2018 and 2019.
Paris police said Wednesday they would ban Thursday's planned protest in the French capital, citing concerns for public safety and the protection of property.
Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu, who met union representatives Wednesday, said a "massive" security operation was planned for Saturday to prevent a repeat of the violence by small groups of rioters that had exposed shortcomings in security measures.
"We are using the legal means at our disposal to prevent further incidents of this kind," Macron said.
"Those who intend to cause disturbances in city centers next Saturday will be prevented from doing so. Tomorrow, we will also have a very detailed update on the implementation of these measures, including anticipation, intelligence gathering and security, not just for Saturday, but also for the coming weeks," he added.
